Seed_Notes: There is some conflicting information in the Project Summary regarding the application rate. The narrative states 'The seed consisted of 5,240\r\npounds of Wyoming and 5,240 pounds of Basin Sagebrush'. The App. Rate is then given as 1.00 lbs/acre which does not correlate exactly.
Objectives:
The objective of this
treatment is to reestablish a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches the
structural and species composition and diversity of the native plant community to help achieve a
healthy, functioning rangeland. Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of sagebrush is important to
maintaining the value of the area as sage grouse breeding and wintering habitat. Sagebrush is also
an important component of suitable habitat for a number of sensitive sagebrush obligate species.
The wildfire intensity impacted existing sagebrush cover which would not recover naturally without
providing additional seed source.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 10,000 acres of the Bear Den Butte wildfire
would be aerial seeded with a mixture of basin big sagebrush and Wyoming big sagebrush in the
winter of 2007/2008 (FY08). This area is in fair condition and would not be drill seeded or
chemically sprayed. This 10,000 acre area would be strip seeded.
Actual_Implementation:
Bear Den Butte Sagebrush Seeding
This project consisted of aerial seeding 5,000 acres out of an area of 10,216 acres. Rate of
application was approximately 1.00 pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed consisted of 5,240
pounds of Wyoming and 5,240 pounds of Basin Sagebrush which was mixed during the loading
process. The seed was applied to snow covered ground in strips from north to south. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding,
ID. Pilot for the seeding was Rob Cantrell. The project was completed using one helicopter and
two sling type buckets. The project was started and completed on 02/18/08.

Contract Cost: $ 13,750.00 
Seed Cost: $ 81,270.00
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results FY09
Qualitative and quantitative monitoring was established in FY09. No sagebrush seedlings were
documented in quantitative plots. Qualitative observations did not document seedlings. The
cool wet weather in June produced heavy cover of herbaceous cover which made observation of
sagebrush seedlings difficult. Monitoring will be continued in FY10.
Monitoring Results FY10
Qualitative and quantitative monitoring documented establishment of sagebrush seedlings in
FYI0. Sagebrush seedlings were documented in quantitative plots at .08 plants per square meter
across all plots. Qualitative observations did reveal some establishment of seedlings in small
patches across the treatment area. The cool wet weather in June produced heavy cover of annual
and perennial herbaceous cover which made observation of sagebrush seedlings difficult.

Seed_Mix_Name: Aerial Seed Grass, Forb and Sagebrush Mix
Objectives: Aerial seed Wyoming big sagebrush, perennial grasses, and forbs to establish a desirable perennial plant community that would prevent soil erosion, reduce introduction and spread of noxious weeds and invasive plants, and protect and restore habitat for sage-grouse and other wildlife.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 23,847 acres of the Blair fire would be
aerially seeded with two seed mixes to reestablish key sage grouse and deer winter range habitat.
The aerial seeding would be implemented in the fall of 2011.
Approximately 10,629 acres would be aerially seeded with a mixture of grasses, forbs and
sagebrush, as shown in the table below. These acres are located in the upper and western
portions of the burn area that are not treatable by drill seeding due to the roughness of the terrain.
Key sagebrush cover was lost across this area and the understory vegetation is expected to
convert to an exotic annual vegetation condition if grass/forb/shrub seeding treatments are not
implemented. Perennial understory vegetation along with a sagebrush overstory is vital for sage
grouse habitat. The rugged terrain is conducive to aerial seeding with mostly small seeded
species because of the high incidence of more productive microsites for seed germination.
Actual_Implementation: Seed was purchased. The aerial seed mix consisted of Wyoming big sagebrush, perennial grasses and forbs.\r\nAerial seeding began and completed on 11/09/2011 and completed on 11/21/2011. The entire 10,269 acre area was seeded. ESR specialists monitored activities and conditions during implementation.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results
Quantitative objectives identified for drill and aerial seeding are:
• For drill seed areas – establish seeded grasses at densities of 4 plants/m2 and seeded forbs at 0.5 plants/m2.
• For sagebrush aerial seed areas – 0.10 plants/m2.
• The amount of bare mineral soil (i.e. soil lacking cover of plants, litter, or biological soil crust) is within 10% of what would be expected for the site based on an adjacent unburned site or the ecological site description.
Qualitative objectives identified for drill and aerial seeding are:
• The majority of desired herbaceous perennial plants are producing seed.
• The plants must also have developed root systems that are extensive enough to provide soil stabilization and prevent uprooting when grazed, especially when soils are moist.

FY12
There were 24 monitoring plots established during the summer of 2012. Cover, density, and belt transect data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1, 2 and 3). Cover and density across the plots was dominated by cheatgrass. Percent cover of cheatgrass was moderate at 11.94. Seeded species detected in density plots included bitterbrush (.006/m2), bottlebrush squirreltail (.58/m2), flax (.006/m2), penstemon (.01/m2), sainfoin 9.03/m2), Siberian wheatgrass (.14/m2), yarrow (.08/m2) and Sandberg’s bluegrass (3.22/m2). Qualitative observations by fire ecologists revealed that fair germination of seeded species occurred in early spring. The latter part of spring was dry reducing growth and vigor of germinating plants. Summer was hot and dry. Competition from annual vegetation is currently moderate with the drill seeded species. No big sagebrush seedlings were detected in cover, density or belt transects.
FY13
The 24 monitoring plots were read during the summer of 2013. Cover, density, and belt transect data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1, 2 and 3). Cover and density across the plots was dominated by cheatgrass though slightly less in 2013. Density of seeded and other dominant species decreased slightly in 2013 probably due to extreme drought conditions. Belt transects across the bitterbrush drill seed area were documenting bitterbrush at .04 plants/m2. Qualitative observations revealed that seeded species were maintaining establishment for the previous year but drought was negatively affecting vigor and spring growth.
FY14
The 24 monitoring plots were read during the summer of 2014. Cover, density, and belt transect data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1, 2 and 3). Cover and density of cheatgrass decreased across the plots in 2014. Density of seeded and other dominant species increased slightly in 2014 probably due to decreased competition from annual species. Belt transects across the bitterbrush drill seed area were documenting bitterbrush at .04 plants/m2.
Qualitative observations revealed that seeded species were maintaining establishment from the previous year but drought was negatively affecting vigor and spring growth. Northerly exposures were maintaining good cover of seeded species. Southerly exposures were more scattered. It was evident that cheatgrass cover is less than the previous year due to drought conditions.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
The Brigham Point Fire (F-369) primarily burned a
cheatgrass/green rabbitbrush community on shallow soil with fairly
low heat. To compete favorably with the expected huge flush of
cheatgrass, a diverse seed mix of only aggressive introduced species
(except Sagebrush) is recommended. A drought tolerant, aggressive
mix is needed to ensure that this area will be rehabilitated.
Tall wheatgrass, Siberian wheatgrass, and Nordan crested
wheatgrass, all bunchgrasses, and pubescent wheatgrass, a
sodgrass, are included which should thrive in this shallow loamy
site. The team wanted to make the mix of grasses as diverse as
possible to simulate natural conditions while still being able to
compete with cheatgrass.
Some Wyoming big sagebrush was lost as a result of this fire. The
entire 2600 acres of the burn will be aerially seeded with
sagebrush. Rabbitbrush will resprout. Wyoming big sagebrush and
Spredor III alfalfa are recommended for inclusion in the seed mix
to provide valuable wildlife habitat.
The seed mix proposed is diverse with a good mixture of grasses,
forbs, and a shrub component.

Objectives:
The goal of the proposed treatment is to quickly repopulate the burned area
with a viable mixture of shrubs and perennial forbs and grasses that will: 1) survive and
effectively compete with non-native invasive species, 2) provide cover and forage for resident
wildlife, and 3) provide soil protection and improve nutrient cycling to establish a viable
environment for the regeneration of surviving perennial grasses. Treatment objectives would be
met when =1 sagebrush per 9 m2 (0.1 plants /m2), =1 forb plant /m2 are established per m2, 1
grass/m2 if grasses were included in the seed mixture) and 50% of the seeded plants are
producing seed heads.
Actual_Implementation:
Perennial shrub/forb/grass seed mixtures were aerially broadcast
seeded in January 2007, End-Product Contract, Thomas Helicopters Inc. Palmer’s penstemon,
alfalfa, blue flax, small burnet, western yarrow, and mountain big sagebrush (mixture 1
developed for elevations above 4200 ft.) were applied to 9260 acres. Mixture 2 (mixture 1 with
the addition of big bluegrass, intermediate wheatgrass and Siberian wheatgrass) were applied to
5555 acres below 4200 ft. in elevation.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Treatment Effectiveness: BLM monitoring crews visited the area in June 2007, establishing and
measuring 9 monitoring plots and 9 shrub density (shrub-hoop) transects. Crews recorded plant
species and density, vegetative cover, and canopy gaps using quadrat, line-point intercept and
gap intercept methods respectively.
Treatment Results: Shrub Density. The shrub objective for these treatments (0.11 plants /m2) has
been met with big sagebrush densities of 1.09 and 0.13 plants /m2, based on shrub-hoop
transects. This includes shrubs that are resprouting as well as those seeded in the treatment.
Buckbrush and bitterbrush were also found in 3 monitoring plots at densities ranging from 0.10
to 2.8 plants /m2. Mix 3 was included in the table for comparison.

Forb and Grass Density and Maturity: The treatment objectives for forbs and grasses were not met.  Western yarrow was the only seeded species observed within the monitoring plots, with a mean density of 16.3 plants /m2.  While this meets the density objectives for the forbs, no plants were observed with seed heads, thus not meeting the maturity objective of 50% plants producing seed heads.  None of the seeded grass species were identified within the monitoring plots, therefore the density and maturity objectives were not met.  However, the overall density of perennial grasses is good at 40.8 plants /m2, and % with seed heads over 50% in each seed mix area.

Canopy Cover and Soil Gaps. Canopy cover levels and gaps between plants were recorded to provide an indication of the site’s resistance to degradation and vulnerability to wind erosion.  As monitoring is repeated, this will provide a measure of how well the site is recovering from the burn.  Soil cover gaps in both treatments are very small; over 98% of the soil is covered by canopy or has gaps smaller than 25 cm.  Increases in the proportion of the line covered by large basal gaps indicate increased susceptibility to water erosion.

Comments: Shrub densities recorded reflect both seedlings from the treatment and resprouting residual shrubs, so it is impossible to distinguish seeding treatment success from natural regeneration. This problem may be the reason that the untreated group (mix 3 without sagebrush) has big sagebrush densities equivalent to the treated groups.  
Grass and forb densities recorded do not distinguish between seedling and older plants.  Identifying grass and forb seedlings is very difficult, so while it appears that the grass and forb objectives have not been met, further monitoring may reveal greater success.  The maturity objective allows us to make some distinctions, but it is too soon to expect this objective to be met by these treatments.

Recommendations:  Monitoring needs to be continued into the future to assess the changes in condition.  Seedlings must be distinguished from older plants to adequately assess the success of the treatment as opposed to natural regeneration.  
Condensing seedling categories into perennial grasses and perennial forbs would speed field work and result in a more useful data set.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
1.  Lands Unlikely to Recover Naturally.  
The wildfire effectively removed all existing vegetation from the burned area.  Most of the perennial grasses, which include Sandberg’s bluegrass, bottlebrush squirreltail, Idaho fescue, and bluebunch wheatgrass are expected to recover naturally, but almost all of the basin, xeric, and mountain big sagebrush plants were killed by the fire.  In addition, the majority of the antelope bitterbrush plants were killed or severely damaged by the fire, and only a small percentage are expected to re-sprout and survive.  Prior to occurrence of the fire, the burned area provided crucial winter habitat for 6,000 to 11,000 mule deer and 2,500 elk.  The southern portion of the fire area supports two populations of southern Idaho ground squirrel, an ESA candidate “threatened” species.  The loss of the perennial shrub component will adversely affect these and other wildlife species.

2.  Weed Treatments.
Invasive species, in particular medusahead and cheatgrass, are known to be present within and in the vicinity of the burned area.  Rush skeletonweed was also noted within the boundary of the burned area.  Failure to locate and control existing noxious weed sites will lead to continued spreading of this undesirable species.  In order to reduce the risk of failure and promote the establishment of the desired seeded species and planted seedlings, competition from invasive annual grasses and forbs needs to be controlled.  

3.  Repair/Replace Fire Damage to Minor Facilities.
The fire caused extensive damage to allotment boundary and pasture division fences and exclosures&* involving 17 grazing allotments, 24 pastures, and four riparian exclosures.

Objectives:
The purpose of this project is to re-establish a perennial plant community in an area that has been invaded by annual
grasses and to allow recovery of the perennial vegetation that burned in the Cold Springs fire. The emergency fire
stabilization and rehabilitation project (ESR) will reduce the risk of invasion of annual grass, restore wildlife habitat,
and allow for recovery of native and previously seeded vegetation.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The ESR plan for this fire lists three treatment objectives:

Livestock grazing may resume once post fire ground cover reaches 80-90 percent of pre fire levels. Perennial key species must qualitatively look vigorous and 50-60 percent of plants producing seed heads. Seeded species must have a sufficient root system to withstand being uprooted during grazing. In the late spring 2003 the mean canopy cover for the three sites within the drill seeded portion of the burn was 12.3 percent.  The composition of this cover was: 1.6% perennial grasses, 10.6% annual grasses, and 0.1% annual forbs.  The mean soil surface cover for the three drill seeded sites was 14.1%.  The composition was 1.8% perennial grasses, 8.8% annual grasses, and 3.5% litter.  The mean density for those perennial grass species present in the drill seeded portion of the burn were: Sandberg Bluegrass (Poa sandbergii) at 0.72 plants/m2 and Crested Wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) 0.03 plants/m2.  The canopy cover for that transect within the portion of the burn not drill seeded was 7.6%.  The composition was 2.4% perennial grasses and 5.2% annual grasses.  The soil surface cover for that transect within the portion of the burn not drill seeded was 54.5%.  The composition was 18.2% perennial grasses, 18.2% annual grasses, 3% forbs, and 15.1% litter.  Sandberg Bluegrass and Crested Wheatgrass were present along that transect within the portion of the burn that was not drill seeded at densities of 1.3 plants/m2 and 3.2 plants m2, respectively.  No live shrubs were noted along any density transect in either portion of the burn. 

In 2002 the mean canopy cover for the three sites within the drill seeded portion of the burn was 15.3 percent.  The composition was: 1.2% perennial grasses, 3.0% annual grasses, and 11.3% annual forbs.  The mean soil surface cover for the drill seeded sites was 27.8%.  The composition was 0.3% annual grasses, 5.5% annual forbs, 14.7% litter, and 7.3% rock/gravel.  Point intercept cover for that transect within the portion of the burn not drill seeded was 70%.  The composition was 20% grass, 6.7% forbs, 10% cryptogamic crust, 16.7% litter, and 16.7% rock/gravel.  No live shrubs were noted along any density transect in either portion of the burn.

Soil surface cover for the unburned reference site was 40%.  The composition of the surface cover was: 1% perennial grass, 1.5% annual grass, 16.8% annual forbs, 1.3% cryptogamic crust, 14.7% litter, and 4.7% rock/gravel.  Point intercept cover for the reference site was 60%.  The composition was 10% grass, 16.7% forbs, 3.3% live shrubs, 26.6% litter, and 3.3% rock/gravel.

The cover data collected within the drill seeded area shows that the percentage of canopy cover and soil surface cover afforded by annual grasses increased from 3% to 10.6% and 0.3% to 8.8%, respectively, from 2002 to 2003.  This suggests that Cheatgrass, the predominant annual grass occurring within the boundaries of this rehabilitation project, is increasing at fairly rapid rate.

Data collected in 2003 from the monitoring site within the portion of the burn that was not drill seeded shows the density for Crested Wheatgrass was 3.2 plants/m2 along the transect.  The Crested Wheatgrass population present in this portion of the burn in resulted from seeding that occurred prior to the Cold Springs Fire.
Approximate 763 acres of the burned area was not drill seeded either because the acreage was in accessible to mechanized equipment or prior to the Cold Springs Fire the acreage supported a robust healthy stand of perennial grasses that would recover naturally if allowed to rest grazing for several growing seasons.  Over the past two growing seasons the pre-fire stand of Crested Wheatgrass located in the southwest corner of the burn and Sandberg Bluegrass stand located in the northeast portion have reestablished themselves very nicely.  The individual plants within these areas are quite healthy and robust in appearance and all have produced seedheads.

In the late spring of 2003 the drill furrows were still visible throughout the 198 acre portion of the burn that was drill seeded in the fall of 2001.  However, no evidence of seedling emergence/establishment was found.  The few Crested Wheatgrass and Sandburg Bluegrass plants encountered within this portion of the burn had regrown from old crowns that existed prior to the fire.  This portion of the project will afford little in the way of grazing value unless further effort is made to establish a new stand of perennial plants.  Additionally, a thorough survey of the entire burn yielded no evidence to indicate any establishment Wyoming Big Sagebrush and Alfalfa resulting from the aerial seeding that occurred in February 2002.

Continued monitoring of this fire site is not recommended unless additional rehabilitation efforts are initiated on the 198 acre portion that was drill seeded in the late fall of 2001.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Wildfire has had a long history influencing sagebrush steppe communities&* such communities depend upon climate, topography, and other environmental factors (Tisdale and Hironaka 1981&* West 1996), and wildfire will continue to guide these communities with future lightning and human-caused ignitions.  However, recent and dramatic changes in fire behavior and resulting fire effects have occurred.  As a result and to a greater consequence, the resulting vegetation structure and function will continue to direct future fire-frequency, behavior, season, and magnitude (Clark 1990).  Recent and dramatic changes in the magnitude and frequency of fire=s influence across many areas of sagebrush steppe vegetation have resulted in mono-typic stands of cheatgrass creating more fire-prone/fire-adapted landscapes (Whisenant 1990, Knick and Rotenberry 1997), including the majority of the Big Desert located in eastern Idaho.
  
Nearly 589,941 acres of Federal, State, and private lands across the Big Desert have burned under severe wildfire conditions within the last 4 years (1996-2000).  On July 26, 2000, three more major wildfires were ignited by lightning strikes across this same general area.  These fires were contained largely on land administered by BLM=s Idaho Falls Field Office (IFFO). This Rehabilitation Plan presents information pertinent to all fires and outlines how the efforts may be combined to improve efficiencies.  

Fire Name		Total Acers	BLM Acers	State Acres	Private Acres
Flat Top		57,477 	41,943 	 2,131		13,402
Coffee Point		72,783		69,141 	 1,850		  1,792
Tin Cup		18,140 	  5,649		     0       	      0     
Total Acres		148,400 	116,733	3,981		15,194		


 
Since 1996, approximately 76 percent of the total 590,417 acres of sagebrush steppe within the Big Desert has been impacted by severe wildfire behavior. Many of the total burned acres have undergone recent increases in recorded fire frequency of up to 3 - 4 fires within a 10-year period.  This pattern of repeated large-scale fires across previously impacted areas within relatively short intervals is attributed primarily, to recent cheatgrass invasions across many areas which used to support sagebrush steppe vegetation.  These conditions represent serious fire and resource management concerns. (Please refer to the Big Desert 2000 Rehabilitation Maps across Land Ownership and Key Sage grouse Habitat (Figure I, III)).

Besides reestablishing the vegetation lost during the fire, two other major concerns exist for resource managers and specialists: 

1)  A pattern of repeated fires across previously impacted areas within relatively short time intervals (i.e. high fire frequencies or short fire return intervals) is associated with the recent invading spread of cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum), a highly volatile flashy fuel.  

2) The productivity and ecological health of public lands administered by the IFFO is in danger of being severely reduced by invasions of new noxious weeds and the uncontrolled spread of established weeds. 

Vegetation recovery.  The three fires analyzed within this document burned relatively completely with minimal unburned patches of sagebrush steppe vegetation.  The Flat Top Fire burned the most completely of the three, leaving only very small, remnant sagebrush patches.  The Coffee Point Fire burned and left a few larger patches, however many individuals burned lightly within them.  The Tin Cup Fire burned across a smaller area with few larger unburned patches.  The patterns showing such complete burns, at the scale they occurred, represent large and severe landscape impacts, as opposed to smaller, patchy mosaics that allow for diverse vegetation structure with abundant unburned islands to provide for sagebrush steppe recovery.

Areas of poorer ecological condition have been identified where rehabilitation efforts (cheatgrass reduction/control and re-seeding) would provide desirable perennial vegetation to reduce significant soil erosion.  The proposed action would also provide for restoration of the sagebrush steppe ecosystem, associated wildlife habitat, and improvement of other general resource values.  Sagebrush cover needs to be reestablished as soon as possible to meet sage grouse habitat requirements.  Strategically placed fire breaks (i.e. green stripping) are needed to reduce the potential for large fires in the future&* such an action will reduce the spread and heat intensity of a future fire and provide for defensible control features across areas of high potential ignition.



 
Cheatgrass invasion. The need exists to reduce the post-fire spread of cheatgrass in order to aid in the recovery of the overall vegetation community.  Cheatgrass is characterized as highly flammable and highly competitive within specific environments, due to its life history and growth characteristics.  High sunlight and warm soils result after the passage of fire, especially when soils are degraded or when fire frequency has been relatively high.  These factors have been found to contribute to the spread and abundance of non-native species such as cheatgrass.  

Cheatgrass further contributes to high fire frequencies, loss of species diversity within native shrub and perennial grass systems, and decreases in remaining unburned patches as it creates a continuous fuel bed.  Reducing cheatgrass will reduce the risk of hazardous fuels accumulation along roads and railroads.  Cheatgrass is susceptible to control by the application of the herbicide Oust@ (Sulfometuron Methyl), an approved chemical for use on public lands.  The expected fuel bed without implementation of the proposed action would be exotic and invasive. 

Noxious weeds.  The productivity and ecological health of public lands may also be severely reduced by new invasions of noxious weeds and the uncontrolled spread of established weeds.  It is believed that most noxious weeds are initially established on public lands from seeds that are brought in by vehicles, hay, heavy equipment, birds, livestock, wildlife or contaminated seed.  The weeds usually invade and first establish in disturbed areas such as roadsides or heavily grazed rangeland.  Among the noxious weeds of concern are white top, diffuse knapweed, spotted knapweed, leafy spurge, Dalmatian toadflax, scotch thistle, musk thistle, Canadian thistle, tamarisk, and purple loosestrife.  New noxious weeds may be added to the list if they are discovered on public lands in the resource area  (Some weed species, such as halogeton and sandbur, are not listed to-date in the Idaho Noxious Weed Law.). 

The IFFO is committed to employing an integrated weed management program using a variety of methods to achieve effective, safe, economical weed control, including: chemical herbicides, biological agents, prescribed burning methods, seeding to rehabilitate disturbed areas, pulling or digging, public education, management as a tool, and monitoring.  Small infestations can most effectively be treated by the immediate application of herbicides and/or mechanical or manual digging.   Persistently perfecting the program over several months or years is essential as various procedures are integrated and knowledge increases. 

Finally, some roads disturbed through fire suppression activities will need to be improved for continued public access.  Fire suppression funds will be used for improvement later in the year when soil moisture conditions will allow for it.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Conclusions
Quantitative and Site Assessment data indicate that the sagebrush seeding has been successful throughout the treatment area. Seeded forbs were abundant in 2013 and are expected to persist until mid to late seral species move into the area (barring excessive disturbance). The low germination and survivorship rates of antelope bitterbrush seedlings may be due to low rates of seed applied as well as substantially drier than normal conditions.

In 2016 seeded white western yarrow and small burnet were minor (2-10%) and subdominant
(10-40%) in abundance at plot FTF6TP01. Forbs were in good vigor and flowering at the time of
monitoring. Sandberg bluegrass and bottlebrush squirreltail were healthy and providing 29.3%
and 8.0% foliar cover, respectively, according to line-point intercept data. Grasses were in good
vigor. Trace amounts of antelope bitterbrush plants was present.
Minor amounts of bottlebrush squirreltail, bluebunch wheatgrass and Sandberg bluegrass were
noted at plot FTF6TP02 in 2016. Seeded Sandberg bluegrass and bottlebrush squirreltail were 4-
6” tall, bluebunch wheatgrass averaged 1.5-2’ in height; evidence of browsing was present on
both species. Trace amounts of seeded forbs and antelope bitterbrush were scattered throughout
the plot.

Objective(s)
1. Attain a density of 1 sagebrush seedling per 10m\xb2 in suitable areas. Conduct aerial
seeding shrub hoop monitoring.
2. Quantitative objectives were not tied to forb, grass, or antelope bitterbrush germination
and survivorship; qualitatively the objective for these groups specifies increasing forb
diversity and establishing early germinating cool season grass and bitterbrush. Conduct
site assessments and line-point intercept monitoring.
3. Greater than 80% of seeded species are producing seed. Conduct site assessments.
Results
1. Aerial seeding shrub hoop monitoring was not conducted in 2016. Site assessments at
plot FTF6TP01 in 2016 indicate that sagebrush were a dominant component of the plant
community (40-100% abundance). On average sagebrush seedlings were 40 cm tall. All
sagebrush were in good vigor. Trace amounts of sagebrush were noted at plot FTF6TP02.
Plants were healthy and 0.5 to 1 foot tall.
Hot Tea FTF6 – ESR Monitoring Report 2016
14
2. In 2016, trace amounts of low and Wyoming big sagebrush were noted at plot FTF6TP02
(see photos below). Trace amounts of seeded forbs including white Western yarrow and
small burnet were scattered throughout the plot. Plants were in good vigor and yarrow
was flowering. Seeded Sandberg bluegrass, bluebunch wheatgrass and bottlebrush
squirreltail were each minor (2-10%) components of the species composition at plot
FTF6TP02. Trace amounts of bitterbrush were scattered throughout the plot; plants were
small.
Wyoming sagebrush was dominant at plot FTF6TP01 with a minor (2-10%) component
of low sagebrush (see photos below). Sandberg bluegrass and bottlebrush squirreltail
were present in minor amounts and were in good vigor. Small burnet and yarrow were
flowering and in good vigor. Trace amounts of seeded bluebunch wheatgrass were also
noted.
3. All perennial bunchgrasses (seeded and naturally occurring) were producing seed heads.

2021 Monitoring: 
This objective was still being met in 2021 for big sagebrush within the Mix 1 treatment area. Low sagebrush was not observed within the low sagebrush seeding area. The southern portion of the Hot Tea fire where low sagebrush was seeded reburned in the 2012 Stout fire likely causing mortality of any low sagebrush.
In 2021 site assessments were recorded and photo monitoring was conducted. Big sagebrush dominated the plant community (40-100% abundance of the species present within the plot) at plot FTF6TP01 (Photos 8-1, a-e) and a minor (2-10%) component at plot FTF6TP02 (Photos 8-2, a-e). Plot FTF6TP02 is poised on a southwest slope and so may encounter early snow melt and hot afternoon sun in the summer; the broader area surrounding this plot on less steep slopes and less harsh aspects contains a greater abundance of big sagebrush (Photo 8-2e).
In 2021 forb species richness was high with 22 native forbs encountered at TP01 and 14 at TP02. Scattered bitterbrush were found at both plots. Bluebunch wheatgrass, bottlebrush squirreltail and onion grass (Melica sp.) were found in low abundance at TP01 due to high density of sagebrush and cheatgrass. Bluebunch wheatgrass, Sandberg bluegrass and squirreltail were all found at TP02 in higher abundances along with medusahead and cheatgrass.
In 2021 plots FTF6TP05 and TP06, which burned in 2012 in the Stout fire, were dominated (40-100% abundance of the species present within the plot) by cheatgrass, medusahead, and rush skeletonweed Photos 8-3 a & b). Native perennial grasses were present in minor abundance (2-10%) and were heavily grazed. Small burnet and bitterbrush that were present in trace abundance (<2%) were heavily browsed. Forb richness was low with 7 species at both plots. Trace big sagebrush was found at TP06. Both plots have gravelly/rocky soil with a dense mat of medusahead litter from previous years. Objectives:
The objective of
this treatment is to reestablish a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches
the structural and species composition and diversity of the native plant community to help
achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland. Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of sagebrush
is important to maintaining the value of the area as mule deer winter range, sage grouse breeding
and wintering habitat. Sagebrush is also an important component of suitable habitat for a
number of sensitive sagebrush obligate species. The wildfire impacted existing sagebrush cover
which would not recover naturally without providing additional seed source.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 4,500 acres of the Hwy 46-MM7 wildfire
would be aerial seeded with a mixture of basin big sagebrush and Wyoming big sagebrush. The
burn area would be strip seeded with the majority of seeding occurring in the drill and harrow seeding treatments. The seeding would be accomplished during the winter of 2006/2007. Seed
would be applied at the rates shown in the following table.

0.90 pounds bulk seed per acre over 4,500 acres. The seed consisted of 2,240 pounds of

process. The seed was applied to bare frozen ground in strips from northwest to southeast. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of
Gooding, ID. Pilots for the seeding were Rod Thomas and Dale Thomas. The project was
completed using one helicopter and two sling type buckets. The project was started and
completed on 01/17/07.

FY07
Qualitative monitoring information was collected during a reconnaissance of the treatment area. Survey of the fire area showed poor germination of seeded shrub species. Noxious weeds are dominant in large areas of the burn. Spring moisture was well below normal levels. Extended drought conditions may have an effect on survival of seeded shrub species.
FY08
Qualitative information gathered in FY08 did not document the establishment of seeded sagebrush seedlings. Noxious weeds and drought conditions appear to have limited success. At this point the sagebrush seeding will be considered a failure.
FY09
Qualitative information gathered in FY09 did not document the establishment of seeded sagebrush seedlings. Noxious weeds, drought, and the re-burn have continued to limit success. The sagebrush seeding will be considered a failure.

Objectives: The treatment objective would be met when established aerial seeded Wyoming & mountain big sagebrush = 1/9m\xb2, and forbs = 1/m\xb2 & = 50% producing seed heads.
Planned_Implementation: A perennial shrub/forb seed mixture comprised of Wyoming big sagebrush, western yarrow, and blue flax will be aerially broadcast seeded over the entire burned area. Because the 2,115 acres to be chemically treated cannot be aerially seeded prior to application of the herbicide, this area will be aerially seeded in the fall of 2007. The remaining 2,080 acres of the burned area will be seeded in the fall of 2006. The aerial seeding on the area where no herbicide would be applied is consistent with the BAR plan for the Emican (CP6Q) Fire, which adjoins the southern corner of the Martha\u2019s Mud burned area.
Actual_Implementation: The treatment area was aerial seeded End-Product Contract, Thomas Helicopters Inc, in December 2006.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Four plots (three in the aerially seeded area and one in rest and recovery), and three shrub density transects were established by monitoring crews in May of 2007. Vegetation data was collected utilizing standards outlined in Monitoring Manual for grassland etc. by Herrick et al. 

monitoring contract.
Results: In 2007 and 2008, monitoring data recorded at established plots indicated treatment objectives were being partially met.  A more extensive evaluation of the aerial seeding conducted in 2008, indicated a higher occurrence of Wyoming big sagebrush and seeded forbs seedlings in more favorable sites, where seed had become buried in ash from burnt shrubs with less competition from annuals.  Aerial seeding monitoring conducted in these sites recorded densities of big sagebrush, 16/9m\xb2 and western yarrow, 1/m\xb2 & 60% producing seed heads.  The occurrence of blue flax was low with a few scattered plants being noted.

In 2009, monitoring plot belt transect survey monitoring recorded seeded Wyoming big sagebrush at a density of 0.1/9 m\xb2 (Figure 1).  No seeded forbs were recorded during monitoring, although both western yarrow and blue flax were observed on-site (Figure 2).  The majority of the site has a fair diversity of native vegetation, which the invasive species do not appear to be outcompeting.  The establishment of aerial seeded species corresponds to the patchy and inconsistent site suitability of the area.  A more extensive evaluation of the entire area outside of the isolated plot location showed results of the aerial seeding conducted in suitable sites recorded Wyoming big sagebrush at 1.0/9 m\xb2, and forbs 0.2/m\xb2 with 50% producing seed heads, based on photos and observations. Even within a general area considered suitable, the establishment of aerial seeded species varied greatly from objectives being exceeded at one recorded site to not being met at another randomly selected site of minimal suitability. Observations made while conducting the more extensive evaluation indicted that overall the aerial seeding treatment was a success in suitable establishment sites.

Canopy cover and basal gap monitoring values provide an indication of a site’s resistance or likelihood of degradation from erosion.   Canopy cover measures vulnerability to wind erosion and basal gap measures vulnerability to water erosion. 
Line-point intercept monitoring in 2007 indicated a 43% canopy cover, and in 2008 a higher 64% canopy cover with 18% bare ground.  In 2008, cover was predominantly native Sandberg bluegrass (41%).  Canopy cover gaps < 25 cm is adequate over 95% of the area; 0.3% canopy gaps were > 200 cm.  58% of the perennial species basal gaps were < 25 cm and 15% of basal gaps were > 200 cm.  
In 2009, line-point intercept monitoring recorded 61% canopy cover with 14% bare ground.  Cover was predominantly native Sandberg bluegrass (18%).  Canopy cover gaps < 25 cm are adequate over 99% of the area; no canopy gaps were > 200 cm.  33% of the perennial species basal gaps were < 25 cm and 20% of basal gaps were > 200 cm.  Overall, the site has a low susceptibility to wind and water erosion. The good canopy cover mitigates susceptibility to wind erosion, and the high percentage of basal gaps < 25 cm and the relative flatness of the area moderates the susceptibility to water erosion

------------------------2015 BLM Contact-------------------------------------
The first aerial seeding (2000) was classified as a failure.... ....so a second seeding was implemented in 2001. Unfortunately, most of the area reburned after the 2006 Crystal Fire, however approximately 4,030 acres of the original seeding remained. Within this unburned area strips of sagebrush can be seen from both aerial photos and when looking north from Fred Butte.
Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of aerial seeding 11,850 acres. Rate of application was approximately 0.25
pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed consisted of Wyoming Big Sage. The seed was applied to
100% snow covered ground, see the attached map for the project location. The contractor was
Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding, ID. Pilots for the seeding were Dale Thomas, Rod Thomas, and
Russ Holiday. The project was completed using three helicopters and three sling type buckets. The
project was started on 2/21/01 and completed on 2/22/01.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
On March 28, 2001, Paul Makela and myself visited these areas to check on early success of the seedings. 
The Brigham Point Seeding, following oust, appears to be coming in well. We found many grass seedlings in the drill rows at one location near the northeast edge of the area. Most of these were about 2 inches tall. 
The Mule Butte Seeding done in 1999 is greening up and still appears to be in fairly good order. It is still too early to tell if we have Secar coming in but the crested and tall wheatgrass types, as well as flax are doing well. We also found a fair number of Wyoming sagebrush seedlings as well as three-tip seedlings. This visit was done along a north-south road running through T5S R25E sections 24, 25, 35. Elk tracks were seen near Bear Trap Lava Tube. 
The Mule Butte Seeding done in 2000 after oust treatment was also looked at just north of the road and west of Crean1 Can Junction about 0.25 miles. We found only a few seedlings in the drill rows but as it is still early, a negative evaluation would be premature at this time. The "native" plants seeded here are expected to come in a bit slower than the exotics which were used on Brigham Point. 
The Whiskey Butte Seeding done in 1999 looks similar to the 1999 Mule Butte Seeding. We will need to wait a year or two before making a call on the Secar in this mix. We noted several sagebrush seedlings near the east central portion of the rehab where none were seeded. 
In the Rice Canyon Prescribed Burn area we looked at Rice (Lindy) Spring. There are numerous aspen sprouts up to 30" tall. We noted that approximately 1/3 of the tips were nipped, probably by deer. 
Also in the Rice Canyon area we looked at the old burn in the bottom of Rice Canyon which was burned, ousted and seeded/harrowed in 1999, 2000. Some seedlings were observed however they appear to be patchy. It was obvious where seed was spilled as there were hundreds of seedlings which at least tells us that they are growing. Most of the seedlings are quite small (\xbd to 1 \xbd " tall). From this area we drove eastward down the road at the south end of the burn area and found many seedlings along the draw/road. Near the southeast corner of the seeded area we looked at the southward facing slopes and found only a few seedlings but once again we saw many seedlings where seed was spilled. We also saw numerous seedlings at the extreme southeast corner at the road junction. Since we were involved with seeding this area, we know that this comer was seeded heavily and harrowed extensively. There is quite a bit of deer sign along the south end of this area and moderate to heavy use is occurring on about 1/3 of the established grasses within the burn. 
We also observed some cheatgrass seedlings throughout the ousted/seeded areas.

10/17/2001: The Mule Butte Fire was the Area's biggest in 1999, totaling 138,908 acres from the Craters of the Moon lava flow heading east 2/3 of the way to the BLM boundary. West of the Arco-Minidoka road little is left of unburned sage or skeletons. Towards the southeast, unburned islands become larger. This fire, especially across the southern half, was where I saw the strongest correlation between standing skeletons or close live sage and new seedlings. Within about 1 \xbd miles radius of Horse Butte are the biggest areas of totally unburned plants. 
The first seeding occurred in Jan. of 2000 on 73,800 acres. When that appeared not to be very successful, a smaller seeding of 64,000 acres across the northern 2/3 of the fire was repeated in Feb. of 2001. 
On Aug. 7-8 and 14-15, we read 103 plots on five transects, directly sampling 21.03 acres. We started using circular plots with a 33 foot radius and plot center spacing of 200 feet along a transect. That plot size has worked well with just one person. Toe thickness of ground cover slows you down a little, but still works well. Stretching one person to cover a 50 foot radius in any area not ousted is too much. Areas of thick cheatgrass slow you down to where the extra ground you cover in a larger plot isn't worth it. Our two-person crew worked well with the full chain radius spaced at 400 foot plot center intervals; and that method became our standard. 
We recorded seedlings in \xbd-inch height classes testing my theory that height results would show two recognizable peaks suggesting some success with the first years seeding. It appeared there were two swells, falling shorter of dramatic peaks, at about 3"-3 \xbd" and at 5"-6" heights. I can't make further conclusions since the majority of the evidence was all found on one transect. 
Over the summer while re-reading existing vegetation transects, we watched for seedlings but only observed any in two or three areas. Seedlings were un-evenly distributed, usually found in dips or drainages of the terrain and often in the vicinity of existing live shrubs. 
I have not been afraid to express my amazement at how fast vegetation has sprung up in those two years, granted that not all of it is desirable. The difference in plant growth, height and vigor in areas Ousted the previous year were also stark. I am not sure I believe it myself, but I saw very deep green, vigorous sage that was 14 "high but assumed to be two years old. Darwin Jeppsen had some interesting comments on his soil moisture observations in those treatments. 
Overall I think this fire had more areas of considerable seedling survival than others and how much to credit natural regeneration versus two years of treatment I can't say. In our meeting the question of any additional treatment areas was raised. At the time I said west of the Arco-Minidoka was the only area I could think of that might benefit but the final decision was not to pursue any further treatment. The more I think about it, the more I agree that two years was enough.

Objectives: Re-establish a population of Big Sagebrush (Mountain/Basin) on 16,946\xb1 acres of public lands burned in the 2000 Oregon Trail Fire by aerially broadcasting Mountain/Basin Big Sagebrush seed.
Actual_Implementation:
The aerial seeding was completed by Reeder Flying Service on 2/6 thru 2/12/2001 using
a Bell 206 B III helicopter with 2 standard seeder buckets. Agitation was used to aid in
feeding the sagebrush and prevent it from bridging. Ground conditions were frozen with
30% snow coverage at higher elevations. Aerial seeding was shut down often due to
adverse weather conditions. ESR plan called for Wyoming Big Sagebrush to be seeded
on the lower elevations and Mountain Big Sagebrush on the higher elevations. A miss
communication during seed mixing resulted in the Wyoming and Mountain being
combined and broadcast over the entire project.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Line-point intercept cover data collected along 5 transects over three sites in mid July 2003 showed that the mean ground cover was 76.1 percent and the mean canopy cover was 30.2 percent. Analysis of the canopy cover data showed that perennial grasses afforded 60 percent of the total canopy cover. Line intercept basal vegetative cover data collected along 5 transects over three sites showed that, on average over all sites, 10.9 percent of the line directly beneath the tape was comprised of vegetative basal gaps greater 50 centimeters in length. Bottlebrush Squirreltail (Sitanion hystrixi), Sandberg Bluegrass (Poa sandbergii), Bulbous Bluegrass (Poa bulbosa) were present along all transects at three sites at mean densities of 0.72 plants/m\xb2, 12.3 plants/m\xb2, and 8.0 plants/m\xb2, respectively. Blue bunch Wheatgrass (Agropyron spicatum) was present at one high elevation (>4000 ft.) site at 0.6 plants/ m\xb2. Crested Wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum), from a previous seeding, was present at the site located in the northwestern portion of the burn at a mean density of 0.32 plants/m\xb2 Cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) was present at two sites at a mean density of 12.1 plants/m\xb2. Medusahead Wildrye (Taeniatherum caput-medusae) was present at the site located in the northwestern portion of the burn at a mean density of 13.9 plants/ m\xb2. The mean density of live Antelope Bitterbrush seedlings, planted in the spring of 2002, at two locations was 0.05 plants/m\xb2 (˜202 plants/acre). No evidence to indicate any level of establishment of sagebrush/alfalfa was found at any location within the burn. Re-sprouted bitterbrush/rabbitbrush plants were encountered throughout.
Line-point intercept cover data collected along 15 transects over 5 locations in mid June 2002 showed the mean ground cover was 62 percent. Plant density data collected in late November 2002 along transects within the two areas where Antelope Bitterbrush was planted the preceding spring showed the mean live seedlings within the two areas was 0.17 live seedlings/m\xb2 (˜688 seedlings/acre). No evidence to indicate successful establishment of either sagebrush or alfalfa was encountered at any location within the burn.
Line-point intercept cover data collected along five transects at one location in early July 2001 showed the mean ground cover was 62 percent. No data relative to the
establishment of shrubs was reported. Cover data collected along five transects at a site in an adjacent unburned site suggested that the pre-fire ground cover was 71.8 percent.
Except for those areas that contained healthy pre-fire shrub populations, the 2003 monitoring data along with observations at random locations throughout the burned area suggest that the present vegetative state of the public lands burned in the 2000 Oregon Trail Fire have is similar to pre-fire vegetative state. The data indicates that the: natural regeneration treatment was partially successful; establishment of shrubs/forbs via aerial seeding (Big Sagebrush and Ladak Alfalfa) was unsuccessful; and establishment of shrubs via hand-planting of seedlings was minimally successful. Cover data indicates that present ground cover is similar to pre-fire. In mid July 2003 more than 60 percent of all perennial grasses encountered exhibited seed heads.

Objectives:
The objective of
this treatment is to reestablish a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches
the structural and species composition and diversity of the native plant community to help
achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland. Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of sagebrush
is important to maintaining the value of the area as big game winter range, sage grouse breeding
and wintering habitat. Sagebrush is also an important component of suitable habitat for a
number of sensitive sagebrush obligate species. The wildfire impacted existing sagebrush cover
which would not recover naturally without providing additional seed source. Forage kochia
would also provide a competitive edge against noxious weeds.
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 6,640 acres of the Owinza wildfire would be aerial seeded with the shrub mix. The mix would be strip seeded across the burn area. In conjunction with sagebrush,\r\nforage kochia would also be seeded to provide effective competition against noxious weeds. The\r\nsagebrush/kochia seeding would be accomplished during the winter of 2006/2007.
Actual_Implementation:
Owinza Aerial Seeding
This project consisted of strip seeding 6,640 acres out of two areas totaling 16,066 acres within
the Owinza fire. Rate of application was approximately 2.06 pounds bulk seed per acre. The
seed consisted of 4,440 pounds of Wyoming Sagebrush, 2,640 pounds Basin Sagebrush, and
6,650 pounds of Forage Kochia which was mixed during the loading process. The seed was
applied to snow covered ground in strips. The
contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding, ID. Pilots for the seeding were Rod
Thomas and Dale Thomas. The project was completed using one helicopter and two sling type
buckets. The project was started and completed on 01/26/07.

Contract Cost: $ 31,540.00 
Seed Cost: $ 131,049.10
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results:
FY07
Qualitative monitoring information was collected in FY07 during a reconnaissance of the
treatment area. Survey of the fire area showed poor germination of seeded species. Noxious
weeds were dominant on portions of the burn area. Spring moisture was well below normal
levels. Extended drought conditions may have had an effect on the germination of species.
Based upon the qualitative observations the aerial seeding at this point may be considered a
failure but a final determination should not be made until after the second growing season.
FY08
Qualitative monitoring information was collected in FY08 during reconnaissance of the
treatment area. There continues to be poor establishment of the seeded species. Noxious weeds
(knapweed and rush skeletonweed) are expanding within the area and are dominant in some
areas. With no evidence of seeded species, the treatment can be considered a failure at this point.
The area will be monitored again next year before making a final determination. The lack of
seed coverage and continued drought conditions appears to be the major contributors to the
failure. The rocky terrain makes it very difficult to apply a seed cover treatment.
FY09
Qualitative and quantitative monitoring information was collected in FY09. There continues to
be poor establishment of the seeded species. Noxious weeds are the major issue currently
impacting the fire area and will continue to be a focus of future treatments. The fire area is
stable in terms of soil stabilization. Recovery of existing native vegetation has contributed to the
soil stabilization. Cheatgrass is present (18% cover) but does not appear to be overly dominant.

The seed treatment will be considered a failure due to the lack of seeded species. Seed coverage
and drought conditions the first two growing seasons appear to be the major contributors to the
failure. The rocky terrain makes it very difficult to apply a seed cover treatment.

Objectives: Rehabilitation by seeding is needed due to the presence of cheatgrass and in order to restore lost wildlife habitat and livestock forage.
Planned_Implementation:
No seedlings will be planted. Sagebrush seed will be flown on separately onto half the native and introduced seeded acreage, in strip and/or block configurations. 
Site selection - Find an area representative of the treatment and soil mapping units. Establish a permanent witness post and describe the location so that another person could return to the area. Establish an imaginary transect line from the post by selecting a compass bearing which will traverse the sampling area. Avoid treatment edges, atypical microsites or crossing into very different range sites. Record transect azimuth in degrees magnetic. From the witness post, photograph a general view of the sampling area, with the skyline in the picture. The witness post may be included in the picture if desired. 
In following years, the transect can be re-sampled with another set of randomly-located plots. 
Seeding of forbs is probably not warranted in that the team has observed that native forbs such as Agoseris, globemallow, balsamroot and others were present prior to the fire and generally proliferate naturally after fire. We thus felt it more prudent to concentrate rehab efforts toward establishing ground cover and structure via seeding of native grasses and sagebrush. 
Vegetation sampling - Beginning at the witness post walk a random number of paces (not exceeding 30) along the transect and place the 9 .6-ft2 circular plot frame at your foot. Record the data. Repeat until 30 plots are recorded. Record, by number of individuals rooted or having > 50% of the basal area within the plot, the following:
seeded grasses by species 
seeded grasses, when species are not discernable 
seeded forbs by species 
shrub seedling resprout species dead shrub burned stumps, not by species live residual native bunch grasses or rhizomatous grasses by species 
dead native bunchgrass tufts, by species if possible, based on size of basal area and presence of nearby live species dead native bunchgrass tufts, when species are not discernable cheatgrass, by density

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
On June 11, 1996 I toured the native rehab area, particularly along the north edge and northeast comer. It is obvious (see pictures) that there is more cheatgrass in those areas that did not re-burn in 1995. It appears that the Bear Trap burn (1995) was somewhat beneficial because it removed the heavy cheatgrass thatch produced that spring due to above normal precipitation (18" for the year). I could not detect any mortality of grass seedlings due to the burn. 
Although the native rehab is not worthy of any awards (at least at this time) it is coming along as well as could be expected ( drilled much less than the 6 lbs. proposed). This year the native seedlings are becoming more apparent and a few set seed. In a few places the drill rows are quite apparent but in general you can't find long rows of seedlings. It is important to note that the exotic grass mix seeded in the NW comer of the burn did not do well at all. It is difficult to find any grass coming up ( other than cheatgrass) but the forbs ( flax and burnett) are present. 
The residual native grasses and forbs are growing well and appear to be undisturbed by drilling (see photos). Globemallow is prevalent, particularly in those areas not re-burned in 1995. 
I was able to find a few sagebrush seedlings but it appears that, for whatever reason, the aerial application of sage was a failure. We need another year or two to make a final call on this. The thick cheatgrass due to the high precipitation. the first growing season may have prevented establishment of the sage seedlings.

Rehabilitation by seeding is needed due to the presence of cheatgrass and in order to restore lost wildlife habitat and livestock forage.

The Point Well fire affected antelope winter range, sage grouse nesting habitat, and two livestock grazing allotments.

A series of large wildfires in recent years has resulted in the cumulative loss of a significant portion of the sagebrush component of antelope and sage grouse habitat in the general area north of Minidoka. This sagebrush vegetative type is also host to a number of other wildlife species including loggerhead shrikes (C2 candidate), ferruginous hawks (C2 candidate), burrowing owls (BLM sensitive), pygmy rabbits (C2 candidate), as well as sage thrashers, several species of sparrow, and other nongame birds and mammals. Presence of cheatgrass in varying densities has also resulted in a shift toward a cheatgrass-fire-cheatgrass cycle of little or no benefit to wildlife and livestock, due to this grass species&$ tendency toward dominance and a resultant lack of structural diversity due to loss of shrubs.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results: 9/29/1993: I asked Mr. Monson at what stage seeded big sagebrush and antelope bitterbrush are able to withstand grazing pressure. \r\nHe has good success seeding big sagebrush and feels it cannot be hurt with good management. Sagebrush seedings can usually withstand grazing after the second growing season. An exception is areas where a combination of heavy wildlife use and fall sheep use occurs consecutively. The seedlings will withstand trampling pressure based on his experience. \r\nMr. Monson pointed out that bitterbrush evolved under heavy use. Use of less than 20 to 30% of current years leaders will not damage the plant. Spring is the most critical season for bitterbrush. During this period it is using a considerable amount o its root reserves for growth of leaders and flower stalks. It is important lo manage grazing use of bitterbrush during this period. After 60% use of a plant most of the leader growth is gone and use is on the woody shoots of the plant. As long as heavy use during the spring does not occur continuously the plants should maintain their vigor. It requires continuous heavy grazing use to hurt it.

Actual_Implementation:
This treatment consisted of seeding grasses and forbs over steep
slopes in draws and gulches within the burned area. Rate of
application was approximately 7.61 lbs bulk seed/acre. Seed was
applied to bare ground. The project was completed using one
helicopter and two sling-type buckets.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring data showed some establishment of seeded plants, primarily Siberian wheatgrass,
alfalfa, and Western yarrow. Sandbergs bluegrass had both relatively high cover and density.
Newly established seedlings were not distinguished from recovering plants that are native to the
site; therefore success of this seeding component is difficult to determine. Unidentified grasses
and forbs contributed substantially to cover. It is likely that some of these were seeded species
and were not identifiable given the fact that they were seedlings at the time of monitoring. A
small amount of crested wheatgrass was detected at locations 001, 003, and 006. This is an
artifact of previous vegetation treatments. No sagebrush seedlings were detected during
monitoring. Cheatgrass was common throughout the burned area and dominant in patches. Rush
skeletonweed was present in monitoring locations 001 and 002.
August 2012 and June 2013 site visits by the fire ecologist confirmed that seeded species were
present in patches and not continuous in drill rows. Likewise, sagebrush seedlings were also
observed as scattered individuals and patches. Gulches and draws were examined to determine
success of the aerial grass/forb seeding treatment. No seedlings were observed and cheatgrass
and other nonnative annuals were dominant.

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The Windmill Fire seeding areas represent some of the harshest conditions found in the Jarbidge
Field Office, with low average annual precipitation and high potential for invasive plants.
However, the ESR project for the 2010 Windmill Fire (FKN4) utilized similar seed mixes and is
showing good establishment (see this year’s monitoring report). It is likely that establishment of
the 2011 ESR seeding was affected by two years of extremely dry conditions. However, given
observations of drill seeding establishment, it is anticipated that cover and density of seeded
species may continue to increase in some areas.

2018 PART 8- MONITORING RESULTS
A total of four monitoring points were established to capture the seeding success or failure of the
Point Well Fire. General observations were collected at each point of species present.
Qualitative Monitoring 2018
Point 001:
POSE, VUOC, BRTE, THPO7, PASM, PSSP6, ARTRW8, ERNA, SPHAE, DRVE, STELLA,
DRVE, STELLA, SIAL2, DEPI, PHLO2, PHHO, GAYOP, EPILO, LASE, LAPU, CHDO,
PENST, ALDE, CORDY, DELPHI. BRTE was present at the monitoring points as well as
SIAL2. THPO7 seemed to be the most successful large bunchgrass at the stirs. POSE and PSSP6
were present with in the sites. PSSP6 mostly in the drill rows. Forbs change between monitoring
sites (Besides SIAL2)
Point 002: Same as point 001
Point 003: High density of non-native species. BRTE and SIAL2 dominated the area. The far
eastern side of the fire had the highest cover of non-native annual species. Some seeded species
were present in the drill rows.
Point 004: Same as point 001

The seed mix used for this project had a variety of grass, forbs and brush seed. The low percent
of bare ground is uncommon after the second year of growth. It is assumed that the low percent
of bare ground is due to the high amount of spring precipitation and because of past ESR seeding
treatments with in the burn area. Also, the percent cover of annual grass is low to average after
two years of growth. The high percent cover of perennial grasses and forbs is a contributing
factor to the lower amount of bare ground as well. In the past, areas that have burned in close
proximity to the Point Well Fire did show high amounts of cheatgrass. The 1% cover of
sagebrush is not uncommon after one year of growth, mainly because it was observed in the
density monitoring and ocular monitoring.

The density data shows the seeded perennial grass measured low and a high measurement of
cheatgrass. The moisture received this winter was well above the average this year and could be
a big contributing factor for these results. I would expect the density numbers of cheatgrass to
reduce and seeded perennial grasses to increase, especially by the third year. The measurement
of sagebrush is a positive result. Wyoming big sagebrush was recorded only this year. Only
Wyoming big sage was seeded, and threetip sage was observed last year but not this year

PART 9-RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
The majority of the fire was characterized by moderate to high fire intensity. Vegetation in the
western portion of the fire was primarily crested wheatgrass from past seedings, sagebrush and
scattered native herbaceous grasses. The understory in the eastern portion of the burn is
dominated by native perennial grasses with areas of cheatgrass. Cheatgrass will continue to
expand and threaten soil stability and biological integrity, if not treated by drill seeding. The
entire area would be susceptible to the expansion of cheatgrass and noxious weeds without
treatment. A high Vole activity was observed in the burned area and surrounding areas. The
outcome for next year monitoring is unknown and failure could be a factor.
After three years of monitoring, it is my conclusion to continue to monitor for seeding success
especially sagebrush and bitterbrush. The moderate amount of cheatgrass after three growing
seasons is a concern; especially at the elevation this project is located. The lack of forbs could be
a factor and this will be noted for future ESR projects in areas similar. Also, the continuation of
monitoring for noxious weeds and implementation of eradicating when noxious species are
present must also continue.

My conclusion thus far is that seeded perennial grasses are present and establishing. The low
traces of sagebrush and bitterbrush after two years is not uncommon and third year monitoring is
essential. My overall observation of this project is successful.
It is my recommendation that monitoring continues to some extent. The presence and lack of
sagebrush observed during monitoring is a concern. Continued monitoring could prove useful for
potential future projects and the continuation of habitat improvement. Also, the presence of
noxious weeds need to be continually addressed until contained and controlled.
It also needs to be noted that over the past few years this areas has been infested with Voles
which may be one factor for the lesser percent of perennial grass cover and lower density of
shrubs. This area is being watched for Vole decline or persistence.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results: 2020: Aerial sagebrush seeding did not meet threshold densities for treatment success, nor were they observed to be common across the landscape in qualitative surveys, thus this treatment did not meet objectives. Qualitative observations found Wyoming big sagebrush at 2 monitoring locations on the Whiskey ESR project area (Appendix 1). The seed source and seed quality of the aerially seeded sagebrush is unknown, and could have affected success rates. Wyoming big sagebrush seed quality is essential for seeding to be effective. Locally sourced seed that is adapted to the specific microclimate will lead to greater establishment. Since sagebrush seed is relatively short-lived, current year seed is recommended (Meyer and Warren 2015). The timing of seed application could have affected seeding success, with seeding occurring in early February, which missed the heavier precipitation and cooler temperatures of December and January. Sagebrush recruitment is highly weather dependent, with adequate moisture and cool temperatures essential for successful establishment (Meyer 1994). Late fall or early winter is recommended for seeding, since this mimics natural dispersal, and increases the likelihood of experiencing snow cover which greatly increases establishment success. Seeding too early in the fall increases the chance of seed mortality, while seeding in the spring does not provide enough moisture for seedlings to become established (Meyer 1994).\r\nWhile sufficient cool temperatures were present in February 2018 when the treatment was applied to stimulate germination, seedling survival could have been enhanced by the longer duration of cool temperatures greater moisture availability in December and January. Sagebrush seeds are tiny and adversely impacted by competition, especially with aggressive non-native annual grasses. Seeding into dense stands of highly competitive plants such as the thick sward of cheatgrass present in 2018 is generally ineffective (Meyer and Warren 2015), and the large flush of non-native species in the spring of 2018 may have affected sagebrush recruitment success on this ESR project. Sagebrush recruitment from seed may also be limited on drier, rocky sites, or sites without microsite heterogeneity that traps snow (such as existing standing live or dead vegetation that is not too dense) (Schuman and Belden 2002, Meyer and Warren 2015). Seed banking of Wyoming and basin big sagebrush is thought to occur to a limited extent, with greater seed longevity if seeds are buried (Wijayrutne and Pyke 2009, 2012). Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings were observed on more monitoring plots in 2020 than in 2018, indicating that some seed banking of seeds from the initial seed application did occur. Further large-scale aerial seeding of sagebrush may result in more recruitment if weather conditions are favorable, but sagebrush plantings or seeding in islands of prepared seed bed may be more successful, and establish a seed source for colonization of the wider landscape.

Aerial grass and drill seeding treatments
Three years post-treatment, the Antelope ESR project area had almost 50 percent cover of perennial grass species, 14.7 percent of which came from seeded species. Seeded grass density averaged 3.9 plants/m2, exceeding goals for drill treatment success. Areas dominated with a high cover of Sandberg bluegrass had lower seeded grass establishment. The nearly continuous sod of this native species may prevent seeded species from reaching bare ground necessary for germination, or because it has shallow roots that may dominate soil moisture resources, provide too much competition once seeds have germinated. These sites also tended to be drier, with rocky fine soils, which may not be as favorable for seedling establishment. The benefits of a continuous cover of native grass, in terms of stabilizing the soil and resisting invasion by noxious/invasive plants, may outweigh the lack of seed treatment establishment.
Aerial grass and drill seed treatments were overwhelmingly dominated by Siberian wheatgrass, probably because of the dominance of this seed in the seed mixes, and the establishment success of this stabilizing species. Native cultivars including Sherman Sandberg bluegrass and Snake River wheatgrass were moderately successful, establishing on a subset of ESR monitoring plots at lower densities and cover. These species were seeded at much lower rates than Siberian wheatgrass.
An established perennial grass community that covers bare ground and utilizes soil resources is better able to resist invasion by invasive and noxious species. Monitoring showed that invasive annual grasses and forbs did decline with time and increased cover of perennial grasses on the Antelope ESR project. Areas that received aerial herbicide treatment in 2017 continued to have lower densities of invasive species than areas that had not been treated. Noxious species remained stable on the ESR project, and new infestations of new noxious species (diffuse knapweed and scotch thistle) were observed. These small infestations should be a treatment priority before they become unmanageable. Areas that were dominated by rush skeletonweed in 2018, showed improvements in 2020, with seeded grass species establishing. It is expected that as grasses increase in these areas, rush skeletonweed will decline further.
Aerial sagebrush and forb seeding did not meet threshold densities for treatment success, nor were they observed to be common across the landscape in qualitative surveys, thus this treatment did not meet objectives. Approximately 21,960 acres was aerially seeded
in the winter of 2019 at a bulk rate of 4.0 lb./ac using a mixture of Wyoming big sagebrush,

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2019 - The 2019 monitoring results revealed that aerial seeding could have an effect on increasing
the amount of shrub cover in burned areas.

Aerial sagebrush
seeding would be considered a success if the density studies on the seeded areas find 40
seedlings per acre, or more seedlings per acre than the control areas within five years. The
grass/forb seeding would be considered a success if a minimum of three individuals per
meter square is observed.
Given that only one growing-season has passed since the aerial seeding treatment, it is too early
to determine the long-term effects (i.e. amount of successful revegetation). Continued monitoring
will depend on the availability of monitoring crews and funding, as time-since-fire increases will
reveal a more definitive result regarding the effects of aerial seeding.

PART 9 - RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
Continue to monitor and start chemical treatment of noxious weeds within the Grassy
Ridge Fire perimeter.
Continue monitoring recovery of the plant community within the Grassy Ridge Fire.
Monitor the effectiveness of the aerial sagebrush and grass/forb seeding and its ability to
reduce recovery times if monitoring crews and funds are available.
Keep livestock grazing closures in effect for one more growing season to allow for
vegetation stability.
Implementation of more control/burned transects to be monitored to determine if all the
vegetation types within the Grassy Ridge Fire are recovering to post fire canopy cover
within fire perimeter. Monitoring may have significant impact as the area recovers from
fire impacts and should be looked at if monitoring crews and funds are available in 2020.

2021: The fire removed existing shrubs that served as habitat for GRSG and other wildlife. The area that burned contained sagebrush and other shrub species at sufficient levels to be considered priority GRSG habitat as well as potential habitat for several sensitive sagebrush obligate species. The loss sagebrush further reduces the overall quality and quantity of GRSG and other sensitive species habitat within the area.
The 2019 monitoring results revealed that aerial seeding could have an effect on increasing the amount of shrub cover in burned areas. Approximately 21,960 acres was aerially seeded in the winter of 2019 at a bulk rate of 4.0 lb/ac using a mixture of Wyoming big sagebrush, basin big sagebrush, streambank wheatgrass, slender wheatgrass and alfalfa within designated areas of the burn (Figure 9). Seed was applied in alternating strips perpendicular to the prevailing winds resulting in a total seeded area of 7,320 acres. Aerial sagebrush seeding would be considered a success if the density studies on the seeded areas find 40 seedlings per acre, or more seedlings per acre than the control areas within five years. The grass/forb seeding would be considered a success if a minimum of three individuals per meter square is observed.
Fourteen plots were located within the aerial seeding area and used to track success of the treatment. While the seed mix was mostly (75%) comprised of rhizomatous grass and alfalfa for site stabilization and big game forage, the primary objective was to establish low elevation sagebrush (Wyoming and basin big) in areas where natural recovery was a concern. While seedlings were documented outside of the transects, no quantifiable data exists to assess the success of the treatment. Based upon ocular observations alone the sagebrush seeding would be considered minimally successful at best, with sagebrush densities ranging between 5-10 plants/acre. Additional sagebrush specific monitoring is planned in the future with the hopes that as those seeded species become more established, a more accurate evaluation on the treatment’s success can be made.

Sagebrush and alfalfa will be aerial seeded.

Information presented at the Sagebrush/Grassland Restoration Workshop in Elko, NV (2002) suggested seed mixes that included >2.0 lbs/ac of non-native wheatgrasses greatly increased the likelihood of non-native grasses dominating the site. The proposed seed mix includes 'Siberian' wheatgrass at 2.5 lbs/ac and tall wheatgrass at 0.5 lbs/ac. We recommend reducing the rates of 'Siberian' wheatgrass and tall wheatgrass to less than 2 lbs/ac for their combined total and increasing the rate of native grasses such as Snake River wheatgrass.

A qualitative summary was written by the monitoring crew after all the quantitative data was collected. The higher elevation points were typically more diverse than the lower elevation points. The appeared to be Vole damage to some of the monitoring sites. Big clearing of vegetation (mainly grass) was cut down. Monitoring points that did not have the implementation of the chaining had higher densities of cheatgrass. Overall there was a good establishment of seeded species throughout the monitoring sites. Sagebrush was observed in the higher elevation monitoring sites. During the specific sagebrush monitoring site, there were little seedlings recorded but seedlings were observed. The lower elevation monitoring sites had little to none sagebrush seedlings. The lack of diversity is a concern, but the lack of annual grasses was a positive outcome. The objective of three seeded grass species per square meter.
The quantitative third year monitoring results showed that there was a slight decrease in perennial grasses and a continued decrease in bare ground. That is to be expected the third year as the grasses begin to produce litter. The annual grasses decreased by only by 3%. Forbs increased by only 1%, but the litter increased by 24%. The density monitoring results show that there is a downward trend in the perennial grasses that maybe caused by the re-introduction of grazing. There was an increase in forb density across the project area. The sagebrush seedling density monitoring also showed a decrease in the density. An increase infestation with Voles was observed during monitoring this year. A large area where perennial grass had been cut down and seeds were missing was noticed. The increase in Voles could be one of the reason a decrease in perennial grass densities had declined.
